title: Singapore Airlines Says Air India Investments Funded From Internal Resources
excerpt: SIA says any further funding for its 25.1% Air India stake will be assessed under its capital-allocation framework as the carrier seeks fresh capital.
body:
• Singapore Airlines told Singapore's Parliament that its investments in India are and will continue to be funded from internal resources, answering a lawmaker's question on September 8.
  • SIA holds a 25.1% stake in the enlarged Air India following the November 2024 merger of Vistara — the joint venture it co-founded — into the Tata Group carrier.
  • The airline reported S$10.48 billion in cash reserves at June 30, with less than S$3 billion in current debt and S$3.24 billion in undrawn committed credit lines.
  • Air India posted a record US$2.4 billion annual loss for the year ended March 31 and is seeking fresh capital from investors as its recovery plan continues.

Singapore Airlines has told Singapore's Parliament that its investments in India are — and will continue to be — funded through internal resources, as scrutiny grows over the finances of Air India, in which SIA holds a 25.1% stake.

In a statement on September 8, SIA responded to a question from MP Kenneth Tiong about whether losses at its overseas associated companies could impair the flag carrier's ability to provide essential air transport services for Singapore. The airline pointed to what it described as one of the strongest balance sheets in the industry.

The parliament question

Tiong's question put SIA's India exposure squarely on the legislative record. Air India, which absorbed SIA's Vistara joint venture in November 2024 to become an enlarged national carrier 25.1%-owned by the Singapore group, reported a record annual loss of US$2.4 billion for the financial year ended March 31 and is now seeking a capital injection from its investors.

For SIA, the optics matter. The Air India investment is its largest foreign equity bet, made with the Tata Group as partner, and any suggestion that it could constrain the airline's core Singapore operations was always going to draw a formal response.

SIA's balance sheet

The response was emphatic. The airline reported S$10.48 billion in cash reserves as of June 30 — S$9.10 billion in cash and bank balances plus S$1.38 billion in fixed deposits — against less than S$3 billion in current debt and a further S$3.24 billion in undrawn committed credit lines.

"SIA is one of the few airlines in the industry with a strong balance sheet... the group maintains one of the strongest financial positions in the airline industry."

— Singapore Airlines, statement to Parliament

The airline added that any further Air India funding would be assessed on its merits — under board approval, its capital allocation framework and investment criteria — weighing Air India's business plan and funding needs against SIA's own cash flows and competing fleet and product investments.

The Air India bet

SIA's India journey began in 2013 with the launch of Vistara alongside the Tata Group, a full-service carrier built to SIA's exacting standards. The November 2024 merger into Air India gave SIA its 25.1% stake in a national carrier with global ambitions — but the road has been turbulent.

Beyond the record losses, the airline is still managing the aftermath of the June 2025 crash of a London-bound Boeing 787 in Ahmedabad, one of the deadliest accidents in Indian aviation history, and the subsequent resignation of CEO Campbell Wilson. Group CEO Goh Choon Phong met Tata Sons chairman N. Chandrasekaran in Mumbai earlier this year to discuss a funding roadmap, with SIA simultaneously deepening its operational involvement in the carrier's transformation.

What it means for travellers

The parliament statement is, above all, a signal of commitment: SIA is telling markets, lawmakers and passengers that it can back Air India's recovery without touching its core finances. For travellers on India–Singapore routes — among the busiest corridors for the Indian diaspora in Southeast Asia — that commitment matters. SIA's service standards have been one of the selling points of the enlarged Air India proposition, and the airline's willingness to keep funding the transformation suggests that bet is not being unwound.

Whether the internal-resources pledge survives Air India's next capital call will be the real test. For now, SIA's message is that the money is there, the framework is in place, and the India investment stands on its own footing.
